name: Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve at elbow)
aliases: ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow

reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: The second most common compression neuropathy of the upper limb after carpal tunnel syndrome
Patients report paraesthesiae of the little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger, characteristically provoked or worsened by sustained elbow flexion
Weakness of grip and pinch develops with wasting of the ulnar-innervated intrinsic muscles, notably the first dorsal interosseous and hypothenar eminence
A positive Froment sign (thumb interphalangeal flexion substituting for a weak adductor pollicis during key pinch) indicates significant motor involvement
Wartenberg sign describes persistent abduction of the little finger from unopposed extensor digiti minimi and weak intrinsics
Potential compression sites include the arcade of Struthers, the medial intermuscular septum, the retrocondylar groove and Osborne band, and the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
The ulnar paradox means a more proximal lesion produces less clawing than a distal one because the flexor digitorum profundus to the ulnar digits is also weakened
Generic management includes activity modification, night-time elbow extension splinting, and surgical in-situ decompression or anterior transposition for progressive or severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: The ulnar nerve is vulnerable as it passes behind the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel, where elbow flexion narrows the canal and increases both intraneural pressure and longitudinal traction on the nerve. Repetitive or sustained flexion, a shallow or unstable retrocondylar groove allowing subluxation, cubitus valgus, osteophytes, ganglia or previous trauma contribute to injury. Sustained compression first produces focal demyelination with conduction slowing across the elbow and, if unrelieved, progresses to axonal loss with intrinsic muscle wasting and fixed sensory deficit.
additionalDifferentials: Thoracic outlet syndrome affecting the lower trunk
Ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist (Guyon canal syndrome)
Pancoast tumour of the lung apex
Motor neurone disease or generalised peripheral neuropathy
Recurrent ulnar nerve subluxation over the medial epicondyle
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to localise the lesion and demonstrate conduction slowing across the elbow
Provocative testing with the elbow flexion test and Tinel percussion over the cubital tunnel
Plain radiographs of the elbow for osteoarthritis, deformity or old fracture
Ultrasound to assess nerve enlargement and demonstrate dynamic subluxation
MRI when a compressive mass lesion or ganglion is suspected
Cervical spine imaging when radiculopathy needs exclusion
redFlags: Rapidly progressive intrinsic muscle wasting or dense motor loss requiring prompt surgical decompression
An apical lung or supraclavicular mass suggesting a Pancoast tumour
Features of myelopathy or motor neurone disease rather than a focal entrapment
Bilateral, rapidly worsening symptoms suggesting a systemic or central cause
reference.prognosis: Early and mild cases often improve with conservative measures, whereas established intrinsic wasting and long-standing sensory loss may not recover fully even after successful decompression, so timely diagnosis is important.
pitfalls: Attributing ulnar symptoms to the wrist when the lesion is at the elbow, or vice versa
Overlooking a double-crush lesion combining cervical and peripheral compression
Failing to detect a subluxating nerve that dictates the choice of surgical procedure
Inadequate protection or handling of the nerve leading to persistent or worsened symptoms after surgery
